title: A contact path for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: A contact path for a B2B SaaS company
excerpt: The contact page should say what happens after someone reaches out, how soon, and what to have ready. The action is a demo, not a ten-field form.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. The article is about keeping a contact path from dissolving into a vague form.
caption: A contact path should stay distinct, the way two inks stay readable as they spread. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a B2B contact page promise?
faqs.answer: Promise the next hour in plain language. Say that the action is a demo, how long it is, and what will be on the screen. Say how soon someone replies, in a sentence the team will keep.

faqs.question: How many fields should the form have?
faqs.answer: Ask for what you need to hold the meeting. A name, a work email, and a sentence on the job are often enough, especially if a scheduler already collects the email. Phone numbers, budget dropdowns, and industry lists can wait for the call or be removed.

faqs.question: What should a buyer prepare before a demo?
faqs.answer: Suggest the step they want to change, the tool that step lives in now, and who will use the product. Three items are enough. They do not need a slide deck before they have seen the product, unless a real security gate requires it.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company contact page should tell an operator who already runs software what happens after they reach out, how soon a person replies, and what to have ready. The action is to book a demo. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them after the rest of the site did its job.

Write the page as a promise about the next hour, not as a questionnaire. They are deciding whether to spend attention. The page should make the spend obvious and small, and it should describe the human on the other side without pretending the whole company will drop everything for a slogan.

## Say what the next hour looks like

Open with the result of the action. "Book a demo. You will pick a time, and the person who runs the call will show the product against a job like yours." That is a promise. "Contact us" is a label with no picture of the hour.

Name the shape of the meeting. The length. The medium. What will be on the screen. What will not happen. You will not be added to a newsletter as the price of the conversation. You will not sit through a deck before you see the product. If something on that list is not true, do not write it. Rewrite the meeting until the promise is one you can keep.

Put the promise above the form. People decide whether a page is worth staying on quickly. Nielsen Norman Group notes that users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that the first 10 seconds are when they judge. A contact page that opens with empty fields and no promise spends those seconds on clerical work. Lead with the hour. Then offer the shortest path into it.

If a demo is the wrong path for some buyers, say who should take it and who should do something else. Customers with an account should log in and use support. Applicants should use the careers page. The contact page can point those people away in one line each, so the demo stays clean.

## How soon, said in ordinary language

Say the response in words you will honor. "You will see open times immediately." Or "A person replies within one business day to confirm." Pick a sentence the team has agreed to. A faster sentence that you miss is worse than a slower sentence you keep.

Do not borrow urgency you have not staffed. "We respond instantly" with an inbox that is checked twice a week is a broken promise on the first impression. This operator already has vendors who do that. You do not need to join them.

If the scheduler is the reply, say that the time they pick is the reply. If a person has to accept first, say that, and say the window. Distinguish a business day from a calendar day so a Friday afternoon does not feel like silence.

Tell them what silence means, in one clause. If they should write again after two days, say so. If a confirmation email is the sign it worked, say so. Uncertainty after a submit is how people book a competitor while your note sits unseen. The page can remove the uncertainty before it starts.

Keep the same promise on the homepage button, the pricing page, and this page. If one page says demo and another says a specialist will reach out in due course, the company sounds like two companies. Choose the true sentence and repeat it.

## What they should have ready

Ask for preparation that makes the call better, and keep it optional on the form. In the prose, you can suggest three things. The step they want to change. The tool that step lives in now. The name of the person who will use it, if that person is not them.

Three is enough. A longer list feels like homework, and homework is a reason to postpone. The call can uncover the rest. You are qualifying the fit, not conducting discovery in a textarea.

Tell them what not to prepare. They do not need a slide deck. They do not need a security packet before they have seen the product, unless your product truly cannot be shown without one. Say which it is. An operator will respect a real security gate. They will not respect a scavenger hunt.

If you need a detail to route the call, ask for that detail and no more. The team they sit on. The size, in a simple range, if routing truly depends on it. Every extra question should earn its place by changing who they meet or whether you should meet at all.

## Why ten fields lose the booking

A long form feels responsible inside the company. Each field was requested by someone. Sales wants a phone number. Marketing wants a budget. Success wants the stack. Legal wants a checkbox novel. The operator experiences the sum as disrespect. They came to see a product. You handed them intake.

Cut to what you need to hold the meeting. A name. A work email. A sentence on the job, if you do not already have it from the page they came from. If the scheduler collects the email, you may not need a form at all. Sending them through both is how a sure booking becomes an abandoned tab.

Phone number as a requirement is a common loss. Many operators will not take a surprise call. Make the phone optional, or remove it. If you need it, say why. "We only use this if the video link fails." A reason turns a demand into a courtesy.

Dropdowns of industries and employee counts rarely change the first call. They change a report. Collect them later, if you must, from the conversation. A required dropdown with no true option is a small insult. "Other" as the only honest answer means the field should not be there.

Google's people-first content guidance is relevant to forms as much as to essays. The page should help the person complete the task they came to do. A form that exists to enrich a database is working for you. The contact page has to work for them first. You can learn more on the call, from a person who showed up, which is worth more than a partial row from a person who left.

## Book a demo, and make the label true

The primary action should say book a demo. Place it where the first screen can hold it. If a scheduler can embed without wrecking the page on a phone, embed it. If the embed is heavy or confusing, link to it with the same label and keep the promise visible above the link.

Watch the words on the button after they submit or confirm. "Done" is weaker than "You are booked for Tuesday. The note is in your email." Confirm the hour you promised at the top of the page. A vague thank-you is how people wonder if the form vanished.

Offer one alternate for the person who cannot or will not use a scheduler. A short email address, with the same promise about what happens next and how soon. One alternate, not a menu of social networks. The alternate is a door, not a second strategy. Keep it in prose under the main action so the demo remains the path you mean.

Do not pop a chat over the form. A second voice asking if they need help, while they are trying to book, is interference. If chat is for customers, show it to customers. The buyer who is new needs the demo path to be the only conversation.

## Route the people who should not book

A good contact page sends the wrong meetings away, kindly. Existing customers go to support. Job seekers go to careers. Reporters go to a named inbox if you have one. Partnerships, if they are real, can have a sentence and a different address so they do not fill the demo calendar.

Write those routes as links with plain labels. "Customer support." "Roles." Do not scold. A person who landed in the wrong place should be able to correct it in one tap. That courtesy also protects the people who do belong on the demo. Their calls start on time because the calendar was not full of misroutes.

If you are not the right product, the page can say so in a sentence. "If you need a consumer app, we are the wrong team." The operator who fits will feel the fence and trust it. The operator who does not will leave before the call, which is a successful page.

## Check the path on a phone

Open the page on a phone and complete a booking with a thumb. Count the fields. If you are annoyed, they will leave. Time the scheduler. If it jumps while loading, reserve the space. If the confirmation is unclear, rewrite the confirmation.

Read the promise and then sit through your own next available slot as if you were the buyer. Did the hour match the sentence? If the call opens with a long introduction and the product appears at the end, the page lied. Fix the call or fix the sentence. The page and the hour are one product.

Then remove one more field. Almost every contact page can spare one. The field you are fond of is the first candidate. What remains should be the demo, the promise, and the few facts the hour requires.

The contact page is also where leftover site habits collect. A long form, a vague headline, a grid of reasons to get in touch. Those are the same mistakes as the rest of the site, gathered in one place. Read [what to leave off the site for this buyer](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-b2b-saas-company) and then delete the questions that do not change the hour.

When you want that path reviewed against a real booking, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Come with the form and the sentence about what happens next. The gap between them is the work.
